lead.name: Team lead / Engineering Manager
lead.contract: In three months, I'll embrace the new dev team, complete an internal audit, and present my battle plan.
months: Present the audit and the plan, and check your added value

weeks.do: Two catch-ups a week with your manager. Informal face time with every peer and every report. Go to every ceremony.
weeks.line: If you don't have relationships, you'll fail.

weeks.do: Product strategy (ask the product lead why, not what), business model, how the company makes money, one or two customers.
weeks.line: Differentiate yourself by showing a genuine interest in the product and business.

weeks.do: Check the roadmap dates against what the team really delivered. Ask how, not whether.
weeks.line: How can we accomplish XYZ within this timeframe? If it's not feasible, what alternatives can we explore?

weeks.do: Purpose, how to reach the team, roadmap, current load, where knowledge lives. End-of-month-1 check-in with your manager.
weeks.line: The team charter protects you from becoming a yes-man.

weeks.do: Trace one feature from idea to customer: processes, tools, OKRs, who decides. Check the channels: public issues, private matters, escalations.
weeks.line: If you're not familiar with how the company operates, you won't be able to see the bigger picture.

weeks.do: Last three sprints and two quarters: share of time on the roadmap, backlog, stalled delivery, roadmap visibility, people.
weeks.line: Teams often spend 60% of their time on non-roadmap tasks, delivering only half of what's planned.

weeks.do: Pick one minor inefficiency from the audit and fix it with the team.
weeks.line: Don't be the person making changes in the first week to assert your authority.

weeks.do: Help each person on the team make one small improvement. Day-60 check-in with your manager.
weeks.line: Support those around you. Without it, connections grow cold.

weeks.do: Ask for the career framework, promotion, layoff and hiring criteria, escalation rules, and when a bug counts as a blocker.
weeks.line: Clearly defining contracts will significantly reduce disruptions for your team.

weeks.do: Two quarters of delivery in numbers, the disruptions, roadmap vs business-as-usual. The two most critical areas and a timeline. Walk the key people one by one before the meeting.
weeks.line: Let me handle this; I'll make the call.

weeks.do: Start the first of the two areas. Ask the team for input; you decide the order.
weeks.line: Be a change agent.

weeks.do: Day-90 meeting with your manager: what you found, why these priorities, what you propose. Then ask yourself whether you add value.
weeks.line: Here's what I've discovered, why these priorities matter, and the proposal I recommend. Are you on board?

exec.name: Director / VP / CTO
exec.contract: In three months, I'll know the strategy end to end, publish my audit, and bring a costed proposal my manager can say yes to.
months: Propose, agree, and set the next quarter

before_day_1.do: Sit with your manager (and the board if there is one) and understand next year's strategy end to end. Just listen.
Propose the KPIs yourself and write your own definition of success, so the review in 12 months is not a fight of opinions.
Agree time, people, tooling and budget in the same room, with the same people, as the KPIs.
Say it out loud: this is my territory, my org structure, my processes, the way we communicate. Agreement in the room is the mandate. Hesitation is data.
Last, once you know what the job really is. After you say yes you have nothing left to trade.

weeks.do: Weekly 1:1 with your manager. One conversation with every peer: what would make you a success from their side.
weeks.line: Just listen to it, listen to what they say.

weeks.focus: Your reports and the level below
weeks.do: 1:1 with every direct report, skip-levels with the level below. Write down what you hear, no answers yet.
weeks.line: After the first eight conversations you'll hear the same four problems in different words.

weeks.do: Where the revenue comes from, what the roadmap promises and to whom, what a quarter of delay costs in money.
weeks.line: Understand the business model and the roadmap before you have an opinion on either.

weeks.do: Twenty to thirty conversations in total. Write the four problems you heard most. End-of-month-1 check-in: what you heard, no solutions yet.
weeks.line: That list is the start of your roadmap proposal.

weeks.do: Trace idea to customer across teams. Check which of your proposed KPIs the data can already show.
weeks.line: If you're not familiar with how the company operates, you won't see the bigger picture.

weeks.do: Across teams: share of time on the roadmap, sprint completion, cycle time, stalled delivery, people risks, org structure against your mandate.
weeks.line: Quick wins and big stones.

weeks.do: One small, visible fix inside your own territory, owned by one of your leads.
weeks.line: Don't make big changes yet: no reorg, no platform migration.

weeks.do: Sort findings into quick wins and big stones. Stakeholder map. Day-60 check-in with your manager on the draft.
weeks.line: Two months of listening felt slow at the time. It was the cheapest thing I did that year.

weeks.do: Three to five changes, each with a cost, a time horizon and the business number it moves.
weeks.line: A proposal, as opposed to a rewrite plan.

weeks.do: One by one before the meeting, then a pre-read. Lead with the payoff, then the dip, and bring any cut as options.
weeks.line: Plan a decision meeting from its end.

weeks.do: The decision meeting. Name the two or three mission streams for next quarter and their owners.
weeks.line: Be brave enough to enter conflict over finite resources.

weeks.do: Day-90 meeting with your manager against the KPIs and definition of success you wrote. Big changes start next quarter.
weeks.line: Here's what I've discovered, why these priorities matter, and the proposal I recommend. Are you on board?

readiness.item: Definition of success at 3 and 6 months, written down and agreed with your manager
Recurring time with your manager in the calendar (twice a week in month 1 for a lead, weekly for an exec)
A list of every peer and stakeholder, with what success looks like from each one's side
A first 1:1 with every direct report booked in weeks 1 and 2
One to two days a week blocked for the audit
Day 90 in the calendar, with the close-the-loop meeting booked
A buddy or a mentor named, inside or outside the company

readiness.lead: The hard conversation you would rather avoid, named, with a date in month one
readiness.exec: The five conversations done, and the mandate said out loud and agreed

team_health_targets.source: Marian Kamenistak's published team-health thresholds (eng-leadership-toolkit MCP)
team_health_targets.roadmap_share: 60% or more of the team's time
team_health_targets.manager_time_per_report: 10 to 15% of your week per direct report
